analysis.one_liner: Requires most employers to let workers earn up to seven paid sick days a year.
analysis.headline: A Senate committee approved the paid sick leave bill in July 2023 with 42 Senate sponsors, but it sat on the Senate calendar for 17 months and never came up for a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require employers with 15 or more workers to let employees earn one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours (about seven workdays) a year. Workers could use the time for their own illness or medical care, to care for family members, or to deal with domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking. Employers with fewer than 15 workers could instead offer the same 56 hours as unpaid leave. The bill also bars employers from firing or penalizing workers for using the time.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly half of the private-sector workforce, and especially lower-wage workers in retail, food service, and care jobs, who are the least likely to have paid sick leave. Workers could stay home when sick or when a child is sick without losing pay or their job, and survivors of domestic violence could take time for medical care, counseling, relocation, or court proceedings. The bill also applies the same rights to congressional employees, federal workers, and railroad workers.

how_it_helps.text: Employers with 15 or more employees must provide one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, capped at 56 hours a year, paid at no less than the worker's regular rate or the applicable minimum wage.

The time can be used for the worker's own illness or medical care, to care for a child, parent, spouse, domestic partner, or chosen family member, and for needs arising from domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking, including medical attention, counseling, relocation, and legal proceedings.

It is unlawful for an employer to fire, retaliate against, or deny employment benefits to a worker for using the time or asserting rights under the bill, and workers can sue or file complaints with the Department of Labor, with attorney's fees available.

The bill covers congressional employees, federal employees, Government Accountability Office and Library of Congress staff, state employees in federally assisted programs, and railroad workers, and it does not override state or local laws that provide more generous leave.

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers, who would bear the cost of paying wages for up to 56 hours a year of leave per employee and of record-keeping and compliance. Smaller employers under 15 workers could avoid the payroll cost by providing the leave unpaid, which shifts the cost onto their lowest-paid workers. The bill phases in under collective bargaining agreements and allows employers with equivalent existing paid-leave policies to keep them in place of the new requirement.

drawbacks.text: The mandate adds payroll costs for covered employers, which fall hardest on labor-intensive, low-margin businesses such as restaurants, retail, and care providers, and could show up as reduced hours or slower hiring for the very workers the bill aims to help.
Employers with fewer than 15 workers may satisfy the bill with 56 hours of unpaid leave, so a large group of workers would get a legal right to time off but no pay for taking it.

Employers may require a health care provider's certification for absences longer than three consecutive workdays, and workers without health insurance face a burden in obtaining documentation, which the Labor Department would have to address by regulation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most workers the benefit is direct and concrete: the ability to take a sick day without losing pay or a job, something a large share of low-wage workers lack. The costs are real but modest and predictable — up to seven paid days a year per employee, roughly 2% of annual hours — and the bill eases them by honoring existing generous leave policies, phasing in under union contracts, and exempting the smallest employers from the paid requirement, though that same exemption leaves small-business workers with unpaid time only.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the Senate labor committee and was placed on the Senate's calendar of pending business in July 2023, but no floor vote was ever scheduled before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the Healthy Families Act in the Senate on May 17, 2023, and it was referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
The committee ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment on June 21, 2023, and it was formally reported and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on July 18, 2023.
After being placed on the calendar, the bill received no further action — no motion to proceed, no floor debate, and no vote — and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill.
The bill had 42 Senate cosponsors, 41 Democrats and one independent, with no Republican cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who do not provide paid sick leave are better off, since the bill died without a vote and no requirement was imposed. Workers without paid sick leave continue to lose pay or risk discipline when they or a family member fall ill.

against.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill but, as majority leader, never scheduled a floor vote during the roughly 17 months the bill sat on the Senate calendar while Democrats held the majority.

sides.party_line_note: All 42 cosponsors were Democrats or the independent sponsor; no Republican signed on, and the bill moved through committee under Democratic control in 2023 but never reached the floor in either the Democratic or Republican majority.

industries.industry: Employers with 15 or more employees (retail, food service, and other labor-intensive sectors)
industries.note: These employers would have to pay wages for up to 56 hours of sick leave per worker per year, a direct cost that falls hardest on low-margin, high-turnover businesses. Their interest in blocking the bill runs opposite to workers' interest in paid time off.

The bill allows them to provide the required leave unpaid instead of paid, avoiding most of the payroll cost, but they still face scheduling, notice, and record-keeping obligations, and their workers get time off without pay.

Existing collective bargaining agreements with equal or better leave are honored, and the mandate only phases in as those contracts end or are amended, so most union members already covered would see little change while the bill sets a floor for everyone else.
